analysis.one_liner: Limits mandatory overtime for nurses at Medicare-participating hospitals and clinics.
analysis.headline: The bill drew bipartisan sponsorship from six House members but never received a committee vote or floor action, and it died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it a condition of participating in Medicare that hospitals, home health agencies, clinics, and other providers could not force nurses to work beyond their scheduled shift, more than 48 hours a week, or more than 12 hours straight, and could not make them work during the 10 hours after a 12-hour shift. It added protections for nurses who complain, required providers to post their policies and schedules, and allowed fines of up to $10,000 per knowing violation. Exceptions applied during declared emergencies. The bill was sent to two House committees and a health subcommittee and never moved further.
analysis.who_benefits: Registered nurses and licensed practical nurses at Medicare-participating facilities gain a federal cap on forced overtime, a guaranteed rest period after long shifts, and protection from being fired or disciplined for refusing overtime or reporting violations. Patients also benefit indirectly: the bill's own findings cite research linking fatigued nurses to medical errors.

how_it_helps.text: Providers could not require nurses to work beyond a scheduled shift, more than 48 hours in a workweek, more than 12 consecutive hours, or during the 10 hours after the 12th hour worked, with on-call and training time counted as work.

Nurses could file complaints with the Secretary of Health and Human Services, who must investigate; providers found in violation would face corrective plans and civil money penalties of up to $10,000 per knowing violation, with higher penalties for repeat offenders and public posting of penalized providers' names.
Providers could not fire, demote, or retaliate against a nurse for refusing mandatory overtime or reporting violations, and could not report a nurse to a state licensing board for refusing overtime.
The bill's findings cite studies that long work hours cause nurse fatigue, impaired vigilance, and medical errors, and note that 18 states already restrict mandatory overtime for nurses.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, home health agencies, ambulatory surgical centers, rural clinics, and other Medicare providers would bear the cost of restricting mandatory overtime: covering shifts through scheduling, extra hiring, or agency staff rather than stretching existing nurses, plus compliance paperwork and up to $10,000 in fines per knowing violation.

drawbacks.text: Caps on mandatory overtime raise labor costs for facilities, which matters most for rural and critical access hospitals and clinics already operating on thin margins and struggling with nursing shortages.

A rigid 48-hour weekly cap can complicate coverage when a scheduled nurse calls out, and the bill excludes emergencies caused by 'consistent understaffing,' so the underlying shortage problem remains even where the bill applies.
Enforcement depends largely on individual nurses filing complaints and on federal investigations, which historically move slowly, so the penalties may be an imperfect deterrent in practice.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — rested nurses making fewer errors — rests on research the bill itself cites, and 18 states have already adopted similar limits, suggesting the approach is workable. The main honest cost is money: providers would have to staff shifts with real hires or agency nurses instead of stretching current staff, a real burden for rural and safety-net facilities. The bill is also a floor rather than a fix — it does not fund hiring or address the staffing shortages that drive overtime in the first place.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and a health subcommittee, never got a hearing, markup, or vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Doris Matsui introduced the bill on March 5, 2024, joined by Rep. Jen Kiggans of Virginia, making it a bipartisan introduction.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction.
In the following nine months the bill's only actions were two referrals to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, in March and December 2024; neither full committee took it up.
The bill expired without a vote when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospital, home health, and other Medicare provider employers are better off, since the bill died and they keep the current ability to require nurses to work beyond scheduled shifts without a federal cap or per-violation fines. Nurses and patients gained nothing.

for.name: Doris Matsui
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap mandatory overtime for nurses as a condition of Medicare participation.

for.name: Jen Kiggans
for.what_they_did: Joined the Democratic sponsor in introducing the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Her committee received the referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; it sat in the Health Subcommittee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received a concurrent referral and never acted on the bill before it expired.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes to measure; sponsorship was bipartisan but tiny — a Democratic sponsor with one Republican cosponsor (1 of 224 House Republicans) and 5 of 216 House Democrats — and the Republican-chaired committees that held the bill never acted.

industries.note: The bill would cap the overtime hospitals can force on nurses and expose them to fines up to $10,000 per knowing violation, raising staffing costs. Its interest in maximum scheduling flexibility runs against the interests of nurses and the patients whose safety depends on rested staff.

industries.industry: Home health agencies and outpatient clinics
industries.note: Home health agencies, rural health clinics, federally qualified health centers, and ambulatory surgical centers would face the same overtime caps, notice requirements, and penalty exposure, with limited staffing flexibility to absorb the change.

industries.industry: Travel and agency nurse staffing firms
industries.note: If providers can no longer stretch existing staff, filling gaps would push more demand toward agency and travel nurses, who bill at premium rates. That is a business gain built on a cost that flows to facilities and ultimately the health system.
